items.abstract: Nine verification reports can represent nine independent observations or nine copies of one. This technical working paper measures how much fresh evidence a recursive learner receives, how much survives five training updates, and when trusting faulty source identifiers increases predictive error. Across 20 paired simulation trials, correct source identification retained a predictive advantage of 11.95 percentage points of baseline risk after five updates. Exact enumeration gives break-even case-corruption rates of 29.5% to 50.2% under two specified fault mechanisms. The eight-page paper includes three figures and reproducible Python experiments. I proudly acknowledge the role of human–AI collaboration in developing this work. Working with ChatGPT (OpenAI) has helped me expand my strategic thinking, examine competing explanations, and connect my proposals to relevant scientific and technical research. My experience, objectives, and judgment guide the work, and I retain responsibility for its claims and conclusions. I regard transparent, rigorous collaboration with AI as a constructive method for advancing ideas that may benefit humanity.

items.title: Ethical and practical challenges of artificial intelligence for sleep and mental health in disability care: a narrative review
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support sleep and mental health care, yet its role in disability care remains insufficiently synthesised. This narrative review examines the ethical and practical challenges associated with AI applications for sleep and mental health in disability care, with attention to both people with disability and disability support workers. Current applications include wearable and sensor-based sleep monitoring, mood tracking systems, conversational agents, predictive models, and workforce-facing decision-support tools. These technologies may improve early detection, continuous monitoring, personalised support, and care coordination. However, the literature identifies substantial barriers to safe and equitable implementation. Practical challenges include poor accessibility, limited inclusive usability, workflow disruption, variable digital literacy, weak external validation, and concerns about reliability across diverse disability groups. Ethical concerns include privacy and data governance, meaningful informed consent, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, intrusive surveillance, and the risk of dehumanising care. The evidence base is also limited by overreliance on general mental health AI literature, minimal focus on disability support workers, a lack of longitudinal and implementation research, and insufficient co-design with people with disability. Overall, AI may offer meaningful benefits in disability care, but responsible implementation requires disability-specific evidence, inclusive design, strong governance, human oversight, and sustained commitment to person-centred and rights-based care.

items.title: Ethical bricolage as ethics-as-practice in criminal organizations. The case of a drug dealing gang
items.abstract: In this paper, we explore how ethics emerge in contexts of criminal organizations. To do so, we carried out a non-participant observation of a suburban drug dealing gang. Resorting to Lévi-Strauss’ concept of “bricolage”, we posit that actors assemble and recombine available moral resources in practice. We found that the criminals we studied resorted to various practices of ethical bricolage, which we define as a genuine mode of social organizing resulting from individuals collectively mobilizing and recombining available moral resources to promote situated ethical practices aimed at designing and maintaining a delineated moral territory. We contribute to the ethics-as-practice literature in discussing how, in organizations lacking social acceptability, ethical bricolage constitutes a mode of organizing, structuring the boundaries of a “man-made” acceptable life.

items.title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
items.abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.

items.title: Evaluating a large language model for radiotherapy patient scheduling under realistic clinical and operational constraints: A feasibility study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Radiation Therapy (RT) scheduling requires coordination of clinical constraints and operational objectives. Large language models (LLMs) may provide a natural-language interface for generating candidate schedules. PURPOSE: To evaluate the feasibility of using an existing LLM to generate RT patient schedules under clinical and operational constraints through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. METHODS: A one-year, three-linear-accelerator (LINAC) simulation included 1400 new patients across 12 treatment categories modeled after clinical practice. Structured prompts supplied ChatGPT with patient data, the current schedule state, clinical rules, and scenario-specific objectives. Performance was evaluated across scenarios addressing weekly treatment-time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap-constrained temporal relaxation, and infeasible request handling. LLM-generated schedules were benchmarked against heuristic and CP-SAT schedules under two objective settings. A six-week retrospective comparison evaluated 2043 appointments against a clinical schedule. RESULTS: 18.4 min while maintaining low overtime. In infeasible request tests, the framework identified predefined constraint violations and returned interpretable corrective suggestions. The optimization benchmarks also generated feasible schedules, but their results showed strong objective-weight trade-offs. In the retrospective comparison, all computational approaches scheduled the workload without overtime; the LLM strategies reduced mean gap by 50.8%-77.1% and increased time consistency from 86.7% to 99.5%-99.9%. CONCLUSION: Structured LLM-assisted scheduling was feasible in the simulation and retrospective clinical comparison, producing candidate schedules under predefined constraints. The findings support further investigation of LLMs as flexible, human-in-the-loop decision-support tools for translating clinical priorities into feasible candidate schedules.

items.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deep Learning Models for Foundational Program Analysis Tasks
items.abstract: While deep neural networks provide state-of-the-art solutions to a wide range of programming language tasks, their effectiveness in dealing with foundational program analysis tasks remains under explored. In this article, we present an empirical study that evaluates four prominent models of code (i.e., CuBERT, CodeBERT, GGNN, and Graph Sandwiches), plus four popular large language models (i.e., GPT3.5 , GPT-4o mini , Qwen2.5-Coder , and DeepSeek Coder ), in two such foundational tasks: (1) alias prediction, in which models predict whether two pointers must alias, may alias, or must not alias; and (2) equivalence prediction, in which models predict whether or not two programs are semantically equivalent. At the core of this study is CodeSem , a dataset built upon the source code of real-world flagship software (e.g., Linux Kernel, GCC, MySQL) and manually validated for the two prediction tasks. Results show that all models are accurate in both prediction tasks. We also conduct a comprehensive, in-depth analysis of the results of all models in both tasks, concluding that deep learning models are generally capable of performing foundational tasks in program analysis, even though in specific cases their weaknesses are also evident. Our code and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/CodeSemDataset/CodeSem .

items.title: Evaluating use of an activity chair to facilitate daily activity engagement while seated
items.abstract: Activity chairs are rehabilitation-grade ergonomic chairs with features such as braking systems and seat elevation. They are designed for individuals with limited standing tolerance or balance. Currently, there is limited research examining outcomes of their use. Our study used a mixed-methods, single-subject design to investigate the subjective and objective impact of activity chairs on activity engagement among adults with standing difficulties. Five people aged 21-65 with disabilities and/or chronic conditions participated, including two women, two men, and an agender individual. Performance measures (i.e., activity duration, fatigue, pain) were reported by participants in daily activity logs for five days prior to and five days after receipt of the chair. Pre-post semi-structured interviews were conducted. Activity chairs were used for dishwashing, cooking, and studying. Quantitative data included satisfaction rating with Wheelchair Outcome Measure (WhOM) and task demand rating with NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). Qualitative data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Quantitative data were assessed using descriptive, visual, and 2-Standard Deviation (2SD) methods. Compared to baseline, three participants had increased satisfaction and reduced pain and/or fatigue using the chair. One participant had equal satisfaction and fatigue; another participant had decreased satisfaction and increased pain. Four participants had decreased total NASA-TLX score, indicating reduced task demand. Qualitatively, most participants were satisfied with seat elevation features but dissatisfied with mobility and navigation. Activity chairs may facilitate engagement in seated activities for short durations when limitations relate to musculoskeletal fatigue and pain. The device’s compatibility with individual user’s abilities and context warrants careful consideration. items.title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
items.abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

items.title: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Label Learning with a Large Language Model for Compound Defect Detection in Rotating Components
items.abstract: Concurrent defects in rotating components produce overlapping vibration components, complicating the recognition of defect combinations absent from training. We formulate this task as compositional multi-label learning and propose a compositional evidence-grounded framework (CEG-LLM). The model uses a frozen large language model as a sequence encoder, with trainable low-rank adapters and four sigmoid defect outputs. Continuous waveform tokens and nominal characteristic-order descriptors represent the signal, while a four-node composition graph conditions label-wise attention. Spectral alignment and compositional regularization guide training, and a fixed template links predictions to structured signal records. On one dataset collected from a rotating component at 1500 rpm, CEG-LLM achieves an observed-state macro-F1 of 0.941. Corresponding values are 0.922 for a one-dimensional vision Transformer (ViT), 0.912 for a signal-to-text language encoder, and 0.900 for a convolutional neural network (CNN). Mean exact match across six withheld defect pairs is 0.767, and macro-F1 at −3 dB is 0.819. A top-token versus random-mask deletion contrast of 0.207 indicates sensitivity to the selected representation under that intervention. These results assess recognition of unseen defect combinations and representation sensitivity within the evaluated operating condition.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

items.title: Evidence-layered spatial and graph-AI framework for immune–vascular niches in adipose-derived stem cell repair
items.abstract: Adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) are being studied for tissue repair because they can affect immune and vascular cells. Their effects, however, depend on the product, tissue, cell state, and outcome being measured. This review examines how ASCs interact with macrophages, endothelial cells, and other stromal cells. We separate direct experiments from observations in human or animal tissues and from relationships inferred by computational analysis. In mouse studies, ASC-derived interleukin-1 receptor antagonist has been linked to changes in macrophage phenotype. ASC preconditioning has also increased cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) secretion. These molecular changes alone do not show that macrophages resolved inflammation. Other studies report vascular responses and better wound repair after treatment with ASC-derived factors or extracellular vesicles. They have not established which molecular pathways cause clinical benefit in ASC-treated human wounds. Spatial analysis may help identify candidate immune–vascular niches, and graph-based artificial intelligence may test whether their cell organization adds information beyond cell numbers and clinical variables. These proposed niches remain research hypotheses, not established features of ASC-treated human wounds. Clinical translation will require a defined ASC product, measurable changes in wound-cell function, adequate tissue perfusion, durable closure, and reproducible safety.

items.title: Executable Verification Framework for Benchmarking AI-Based Decision Support in Physically Network-Constrained Energy Systems
items.abstract: Benchmarks of inverter-based power grids that use machine learning (ML), large language models (LLMs), and learning-based inverter control can be misleading when fluent responses are operationally infeasible, judge-based scores are biased, or forecast-accuracy metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) do not reflect reserve and dispatch consequences. This study introduces VERITAS-GridBench, an operationally grounded benchmark in which decision-support outputs are evaluated against simulator/optimizer-based "Executable Truth" using explicit feasibility and constraint-violation measures. The framework combines tool verification, rule-based checks, and calibrated multi-judge semantic assessment through Triangulated Scoring, while also incorporating reproducibility, contamination control, domain-shift testing, and a Forecast-to-Operations (F2O) pathway. The experiments compare judge-only, multi-judge, and triangulated evaluation for power-system decision support and compare representative statistical, machine-learning, sequence, convolutional, and transformer forecasting models after their forecasts are propagated to reserve and dispatch calculations. The results show that judge-only scoring can reward fluent but infeasible actions, whereas tool-verified triangulation markedly increases feasibility and reduces unsafe wins and constraint violations. The forecasting results further show that lower MAE does not necessarily imply lower operational cost or risk. These findings support end-to-end evaluation in which model quality is judged by both predictive performance and physically executable grid outcomes.

items.title: Exercise, Diet, and the Human Gut Microbiome: Evidence on Training, Intestinal Barrier Function, and Performance
items.abstract: Exercise and the gut microbiome interact through diet, intestinal physiology, microbial metabolism, and host immune responses. Cross-sectional studies consistently find differences in the microbiome of athletes compared to less active adults, but athletes also differ in food intake and body composition. Some human intervention studies indicate that exercise can modify fecal microbial composition and function, but responses are heterogeneous and detectable changes are not consistently observed. Extended, vigorous exercise—particularly in the heat—can temporarily compromise gut barrier in-tegrity, though these short-term disturbances are distinct from long-term microbiome adaptations. Short-chain fatty acids and other microbial metabolites provide plausible links to skeletal muscle and immune function. However, promising mechanistic experiments in animals have not yet translated into consistent evidence that manipulating specific microbes improves human performance. This brief narrative review discusses the human data linking exercise, diet, and the gut microbiome. Sustained exercise and a varied diet rich in plant fibers and polyphenols may support durable gut microbial responses, but the exposure duration required for lasting change remains uncertain. Repeated sam-pling over long time periods, dietary assessment, and functional measurements remain necessary before recommending precision microbiome interventions for athletes.

items.title: Explainable AI in Medical Tasks: A Systematic Review of Methods, Applications, and Modalities of Explanation
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical tasks has introduced powerful tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning, yet the opacity of many deep learning systems has limited their acceptance in clinical environments where trust, accountability, and interpretability are essential. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses these concerns by revealing the reasoning behind AI-driven decisions. This systematic review examines XAI methods applied to medical tasks, focusing on how explanations are generated and delivered through visual, textual, counterfactual, example-based, and multimodal formats. Drawing on a structured search of six databases covering literature published between 2020 and March 2026, we analyzed 309 studies, categorizing state-of-the-art techniques by their underlying algorithms, explanation formats, and clinical applicability. Visual explanations such as saliency maps and Grad-CAM predominate in medical imaging, whereas textual, counterfactual, example-based, and multimodal methods are increasingly applied to clinical prediction, decision support, and automated report generation. We further examine benchmark datasets, evaluation practices, and empirical studies assessing explanation quality, interpretability, and user trust, and highlight ethical considerations including fairness, bias, and transparency in deployment. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying gaps, this review aims to support the development of more interpretable, trustworthy, and human-centered AI systems for healthcare.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Cognitive Workload Assessment: Methods, Evidence, and Human-Centered Evaluation
items.abstract: Cognitive workload models now draw on eye movements, brain activity, cardiovascular variation, electrodermal responses, and patterns of interaction. Their accuracy can be impressive, yet accuracy alone says little about whether the model has captured workload, memorized a participant or task, or produced an explanation that a person can safely use. This critical narrative review examines that problem across cognitive science, neuroergonomics, physiological computing, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Particular attention is given to construct definition, signal-specific confounding, participant-wise validation, and the gap between plausible and faithful explanations. The review develops TRACE-WL: Theoretical alignment, Reliable validation, Attribution fidelity, Cognitive usability, and Ecological robustness. These five requirements link the psychological claim to the validation design and, ultimately, to the conditions of use. The literature indicates that predictive performance and explanation quality must be tested separately. It also cautions against treating feature importance as evidence of a cognitive mechanism without convergent measurements or intervention. TRACE-WL offers a structured way to judge workload systems intended for education, healthcare, transportation, and other human-machine settings.

items.title: Exploring chronic illness experiences using AI-assisted qualitative analysis: an exploratory study
items.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the main issues patients’ experience while managing their chronic illness by using a large language model (LLM), an artificial intelligence system trained to process human-like text to examine qualitative interview data. This LLM-assisted approach allows for more efficient and nuanced identification of central themes, complementing traditional qualitative approaches. Thirty participants with various chronic conditions were interviewed, and the transcripts were analyzed using an LLM to identify key themes. A correlation analysis was conducted to select weakly correlated themes, indicating limited overlap between themes within the final set, for in-depth exploration. Content domains were then created by grouping related themes based on predefined criteria. The LLM assigned intensity scores for all 46 themes. Variation was observed in how themes were expressed within this exploratory sample of older adults with multimorbidity. Correlation analysis identified patterns of co-occurrence, from which six content domains were created. These domains represent model-derived groupings rather than validated constructs. This study outlines a structured approach for AI-assisted qualitative analysis. LLM-generated scores reflect model interpretation rather than direct patient-reported burden and should be interpreted descriptively. Further validation, including comparison with human coding, is needed before clinical use.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content (AIGC) introduces dynamic reference perspectives that enrich traditional fine-art education. To explore this potential, we conducted a formative inquiry and an exploratory in-class workshop with 8 art-education professionals and 30 primary students to compare two AI-supported observation modes: Generative 2D and Generative Spatial (3D) Observation. Drawing on expert assessments of student drawings and qualitative accounts of their creative experiences, our findings reveal distinct differences in how 2D and 3D generative tools shape students’ observational behaviors and creative processes. The study offers preliminary, design-oriented considerations for integrating these distinct generative tools into art classrooms while preserving active, hands-on drawing practices.

items.title: Exposure to biological hazards and associated factors among nurses and midwives working in Bale zones public hospitals, Southeast Ethiopia
items.abstract: Occupational exposure to biological hazards is an important occupational health concern among healthcare workers, particularly nurses and midwives who frequently perform procedures involving blood, body fluids, and sharp instruments. However, evidence on the broader range of biological hazard exposures among nurses and midwives in public hospitals of Bale and East Bale Zones is limited. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the prevalence of exposure to biological hazards and associated factors among nurses and midwives working in public hospitals of Bale and East Bale Zones, Southeast Ethiopia. An institution-based cross-sectional study design was conducted involving 407 Nurses and Midwives working in public hospitals of Bale zones. Participants were selected using simple random sampling. Data were collected using the Kobo Android application and analysed using SPSS statistics version 27. Binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify variables associated with biological hazard exposure. Adjusted odds ratio (AOR) with a 95% confidence interval were used to assess associations, and statistical significance was declared at p < 0.05. Overall, 68.6% (95% CI: 63.6–73.0) of nurses and midwives reported at least one occupational exposure to a biological hazard during their professional lifetime career. Recapping needles after use (AOR = 2.08, 95% CI: 1.16–3.74), lack of training on infection prevention (AOR = 2.78, 95% CI: 1.61–4.79), working > 40 h per week (AOR = 4.57, 95% CI: 2.41–8.67), lack of safety guideline at working unit (AOR = 3.80, 95% CI: 1.91–7.58) and having work experience of less than five year (AOR = 2.21, 95% CI: 1.16–4.24) were significantly associated with exposure to biological hazards. The findings of this study revealed the high prevalence of exposure to biological hazards among nurses and midwives in the study area compared to previous studies conducted in the country. Therefore, providing training on infection prevention, establishing clear safety guidelines, and effectively managing working hours are crucial steps for enhancing occupational safety and improving healthcare outcomes.

items.title: Fact-Checking: A Survey on Content Verification in the Age of AI
items.abstract: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.

items.title: Factors Affecting the Academic Engagement of Junior High School Learners in the ARAL Program: A Correlational Analysis
items.abstract: This study examined basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration in relation to multidimensional academic engagement among junior high school learners in the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program and sought to inform a guidance intervention. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational design, it surveyed all 91 ARAL learners at Zosimo A. Gulle Memorial National High School, Talibon, Bohol, during Academic Year 2025–2026 through complete enumeration. Adapted psychological-needs and student-engagement questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson product–moment correlation. Learners reported high psychological need satisfaction (M = 4.08), with relatedness strongest, alongside high need frustration (M = 3.56), driven principally by autonomy frustration (M = 4.14). Overall academic engagement was high (M = 3.52), although emotional engagement (M = 3.27) was moderate relative to behavioral (M = 3.67) and cognitive engagement (M = 3.61). Neither need satisfaction (r = 0.168, p = 0.111) nor frustration (r = 0.103, p = 0.333) showed a statistically significant relationship with overall engagement. Thus, reported participation and learning strategies coexisted with perceived pressure and limited emotional enthusiasm, without establishing causal explanations. The study recommends implementing and evaluating a data-driven guidance and counseling plan emphasizing learner choice, supportive tutoring, peer interaction, and psychosocial monitoring. Findings are limited by a single-school cohort, adapted self-report measures, and correlational design. This localized evidence supports sustainable, learner-centered academic recovery and guidance planning aligned with SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

items.title: Factors Associated with Perceived Anticipatory Organizational Socialization Among Nursing Students: Self-Leadership, Person-Centered Care, and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Perceived anticipatory organizational socialization may help nursing students prepare for the transition to professional practice. Guided by the newcomer adjustment model, this study examined the associations of self-leadership, person-centered care, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) with organizational socialization among nursing students. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 142 third- and fourth-year nursing students from two programs in the Republic of Korea completed an online questionnaire; after the exclusion of 11 respondents with missing or invalid covariate responses, 131 were analyzed. Data were analyzed using Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple linear regression. Results: Organizational socialization was correlated with self-leadership (r = 0.62, p < 0.001) and person-centered care (r = 0.34, p < 0.001), but not with attitudes toward AI (r = 0.13, p = 0.148). After adjustment for year of study and major satisfaction, only self-leadership was independently associated with organizational socialization (β = 0.505, p < 0.001); the final model explained 43.9% of the variance. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent findings for self-leadership. Conclusions: Self-leadership was the characteristic most closely associated with nursing students' perceived preparedness for organizational adaptation, whereas general attitudes toward AI were not. Self-leadership development is a candidate target for educational interventions; longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine whether it supports actual adaptation after employment.

items.title: Factors associated with road traffic injury severity in Oman: a cross-sectional analysis of national data, 2018–2024
items.abstract: Road traffic crashes (RTCs) remain a leading cause of death and disability globally. In Oman, although the number of road traffic deaths has declined over the past decade, road traffic injuries (RTIs) continue to be an important public health concern. This study aimed to identify factors associated with injury severity among individuals recorded in police RTC reports in Oman between 2018 and 2024. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using data from the Royal Oman Police (ROP) national RTC database (1 January 2018 to 31 December 2024). The unit of analysis was the individual recorded in an RTC report, and the outcome was injury severity, categorised as none/mild, moderate, or severe/fatal. Multinomial logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) for sociodemographic, road-user, vehicle and crash characteristics; a sensitivity model additionally adjusted for governorate, year, day of the week and time of day. Of 30,307 individuals, 12,405 (40.9%) had none/mild, 12,616 (41.6%) moderate and 5,286 (17.4%) severe/fatal injuries (11.9% died). Most were male (80.9%), aged 25–39 years (43.5%) and Omani (72.9%). For severe/fatal versus none/mild injury, odds were higher for motorcycle/bicycle riders than public transport occupants (AOR = 7.40, 95% CI: 5.50–9.95) and for males than females (AOR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.32–1.65), and lower for Omani versus non-Omani individuals (AOR = 0.79), employed versus non-employed individuals (AOR = 0.69) and those aged <25 versus ≥40 years (AOR = 0.61). Pedestrians had the highest odds, but uninjured passengers and pedestrians were not recorded, so these estimates should be interpreted cautiously. Compared with external factors, risky driving was associated with severe/fatal injury (AOR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.02–1.48), and human factors with moderate injury only (AOR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.01–1.38). In the sensitivity model, night-time crashes (00:00–05:59 vs. 06:00–11:59; AOR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.15–1.46) and Al Wusta Governorate (vs. Muscat; AOR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.58–2.33) had higher odds of severe/fatal injury. Injury severity among individuals recorded in RTC reports in Oman was associated with road-user type, vehicle type, reported crash cause, sex, age, nationality, employment, governorate, year and time of day. Pedestrians, motorcyclists and cyclists, males, older and non-Omani individuals are priority groups for prevention. Protecting vulnerable road users, strengthening licensing and enforcement, and improving emergency response could reduce severe RTIs in Oman.

items.title: Factors influencing attending rounding practices with learners: A rapid qualitative study of hospitalist perspectives
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Attending rounds have shifted over the years from predominantly occurring at the bedside to conference rooms and hallways. Multiple causal factors have been cited, including resident duty hour restrictions, introduction of the electronic medical record, and the coronavirus-19 pandemic. OBJECTIVE: To characterize factors contributing to hospitalist decisions surrounding rounding style choices. DESIGN: Qualitative analysis of focus groups. PARTICIPANTS: Hospital medicine clinicians. APPROACH: A survey was initially administered to capture participant demographics and typical rounding format. Focus group data were analyzed using a rapid qualitative method. Data from recordings and field notes were entered into templated summaries and then organized into a matrix to identify recurring themes and sub-themes. Themes were refined through iterative group discussion and member checking. KEY RESULTS: Across five focus groups, there were 35 individuals and 27 survey responses (77% response rate). Survey respondents, on average, spent most of their time using hallway (49.4%) or card flipping rounds (38.6%). Our qualitative analysis revealed three primary themes: (1) Human factors shape when different rounding styles are most effective, (2) Systemic factors constrain rounding style choices, (3) Hospitalist rounding practices do not always align with personal preferences. CONCLUSIONS: While hospitalists agreed on the importance of bedside skill development and patient-centered care, hospitalists viewed rounds as an interplay between multiple individuals, their needs, and systemic factors, driving when different rounding styles were most beneficial. Participants emphasized a need for flexibility to meet variable rounding goals.

items.title: Factors, benefits, and barriers influencing the adoption of AI tools and software developers’ perceptions of AI tools’ impact on software sustainability.
items.abstract: The adoption of AI-based code assistants like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot is increasingly popular among software developers, aiming to enhance coding efficiency and automate routine tasks. Nevertheless, there is limited empirical data on how these tools affect software quality attributes. For instance, while productivity may improve from a resource standpoint, code quality remains largely unchanged. This research explores how AI-supported development tools influence the sustainability of Scrum-based projects, i.e., software code quality and developer productivity. It employs a mixed-method approach, including a systematic review of 24 studies and 11 semi-structured interviews with experienced industry software developers. The results show that AI tools can contribute to various aspects of software quality, such as higher code consistency, greater maintainability, and improved defect detection and testing. The characteristics of automated code generation and code suggestions, as well as the generation of test cases through AI, were found to reduce development time and cognitive load and to encourage higher-quality outputs. Nevertheless, issues of reliability, security, and accuracy of code produced by AI, especially in complex development cases, still need to be addressed, and human supervision and validation must be ongoing, e.g., AI generates code which is hard to maintain, or AI produces code so fast and so much in quantity that humans do not have enough motivation and interest. The research also mentions that AI-assisted development assists sustainable software engineering by maximising resource usage, minimising reuse, and enhancing long-term code quality. This study offers a contribution to the further study of the role of AI in current software engineering and useful insights on the implementation of AI tools in quality-oriented software development by empirically correlating AI tool adoption with software quality results. Future research should focus on quantitatively assessing the effects of AI tools on software quality, using standardised measures such as defect rates, code quality scores, and test coverage. It would also be informative to conduct comparative research on various AI tools in different development settings.

items.title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
items.abstract: Public institutions increasingly procure AI systems whose design they cannot inspect or change. In higher education, proprietary Early Warning Systems (EWS) leave colleges with few options beyond adjusting model outputs to address inequity. This raises a CSCW question: how is fairness work coordinated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students with unequal power to change these systems? Using student records from a public college in Ontario, Canada, we evaluate six post-hoc fairness interventions on a research EWS under simulated procurement constraints. We compare fairness, accuracy, and demographic disparities, introducing error-type profiling to trace how interventions redistribute false positives and false negatives. Interventions redistributed disparities without consistently reducing them. Two implementations favoured already-advantaged groups because they used group size to define disadvantage; small, marginalized groups remained poorly served. These findings show how procurement constraints and implementation choices shape the possibilities for fairness work. We call the resulting condition fairness theatre : dashboard metrics converge while groups’ error burdens persist or worsen.

items.title: Fault Diagnosis of Ball Bearings Using Fast Continuous Wavelet Transform and XGBoost on a Multi-Condition Acoustic Dataset
items.abstract: Reliable fault diagnosis of rotating machinery, particularly ball bearings, is critical to ensuring operational safety and minimizing downtime. While acoustic signals provide rich diagnostic information, Artificial Intelligence (AI) models often suffer from overly optimistic metrics due to data leakage during preprocessing and splitting stages. This study presents a robust fault diagnosis framework with minimized leakage risk, using a multi-condition acoustic dataset. To completely eliminate leakage, a strict evaluation pipeline is implemented: (i) window-wise normalization is applied to each raw signal window prior to the Fast Continuous Wavelet Transform (fCWT) to prevent information sharing between windows, and (ii) data partitioning is strictly managed via Group Shuffle Split (GSS) and Stratified Group K-Fold (SGKF) cross-validation, ensuring that signals from the same recording do not span across training and test splits. Time–frequency features extracted directly from fCWT coefficients are processed using Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), which serves a dual purpose as an embedded feature selection mechanism and the core classifier. The framework achieves realistic and generalizable performance under distinct operational speeds (800, 1000, and 1200 RPM) and load conditions (0%, 15%, and 30%), yielding an F-score of 99.81% under GSS and a mean F-score of 99.35% across SGKF cross-validation, providing a trustworthy benchmark for health monitoring.

items.title: Financial large language models in manufacturing supplier relationship management: applications, limits, and human-AI decision-making
items.abstract: As Industry 4.0 is coming, Manufacturers need to evaluate suppliers with limited staff and incomplete information. Smaller suppliers may be particularly difficult to assess: their records are less standardized, and limited access to finance can obscure their capacity to fulfil orders. This paper examines whether Financial Large Language Models (FinLLMs), including FinGPT and BloombergGPT, can assist Supplier Relationship Management (SRM). It synthesizes research on quality-management workloads, supplier credit assessment, document processing, and supplier discovery, and considers the applications and limitations of the two models as representative cases. The review identifies four possible uses: extracting risk signals from text, combining textual and relational data for credit assessment, reading engineering documents, and finding suppliers through graph-based search. It also identifies limits in process-specific knowledge, numerical reasoning, confidence calibration, and the currency and coverage of training data. To clarify who should act on model outputs, the paper proposes a "boss-employee" framework organized around task division, decision authority, and calibration through human review. The framework treats AI as support for procurement staff rather than a substitute for their final judgement. It remains conceptual and requires testing in manufacturing settings.

items.title: Foresight Workshop VET 2035: Documentation and retrospective of an expert panel on vocational education and training in the construction sector
items.abstract: In December 2020, an international panel of 25 experts from 14 countries met online for two days to assess developments in the construction sector and to draft road maps for vocational education and training (VET) up to 2035. The workshop was held as part of the European Vocational Skills Week 2020. Its results were saved as whiteboard exports. This report documents the procedure, the panel and the results. It is based on a complete transcription of all exports, which is included as an appendix. The findings show that the panel used developments in the sector mainly as a starting point to discuss how, where and for whom learning should be organized. Recurring elements are a single access point to training, the recognition of short learning units across Europe, reliable funding and the value of skills for clients and workers. Although the workshop did not set up a group for the dimension „Individual“, the full coding assigns 25 of the 235 original contributions to that dimension, while the category for teachers and trainers as the subject of a contribution remains empty. A retrospective from 2026 compares the results with later developments. Several needs named by the panel have since been taken up in European policy. Generative artificial intelligence, however, does not appear on any board, and the coding of the corpus confirms this: none of the 235 original contributions names analytical or generative AI explicitly, while eight name automation, robotics or data without any method and are therefore technological connection points rather than references to AI. The report closes with the limitations of the documentation and links to related work.

items.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

items.title: Foundation Models for Medical Image Segmentation Across Centers
items.abstract: Foundation models provide reusable representations, promptable interfaces and volumetric priors for medical image segmentation. Translating these capabilities into reliable performance at a new hospital requires attention to imaging variation, task definitions and the information available for adaptation. This critical narrative review focuses on organ and lesion segmentation in computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. It examines three connected questions: how transferable segmentation capabilities are formed, how adaptation mechanisms address differences between centers, and which external results support practical model selection. Pretraining objectives, dense prediction interfaces, support examples and spatial modeling are compared as complementary sources of capability. Transfer strategies are then organized by access to target images, training and validation labels, and case-specific interaction, with separate consideration of parameter, representation and input optimization at test time. Evidence from center-held-out studies, external disease cohorts and human annotation experiments shows that appropriate initialization, task adaptation and interaction can yield useful gains. Their interpretation depends on the comparator, the information supplied and the unit of evaluation. Accuracy, difficult cases, prompting requirements and the cost of the complete workflow therefore need to be considered together. An information-conditional framework links changes between centers to capability requirements, available resources, adaptation mechanisms and external benefit. This framework supports study design, model comparison and annotation resource allocation for deployment at new centers.

items.title: From AI-Assisted Work to Verifiable Learning: Critical AI Use and Assessment Redesign Across Five Higher Education Cohorts
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges whether submitted academic work can serve as credible evidence of individual learning. This study examined GenAI use, critical AI practices, active teaching and assessment strategies, and self-reported verifiable-learning capabilities in higher education. A convergent post-intervention mixed-methods design involved 94 undergraduates from five cohorts, three disciplinary contexts, and two academic stages at a public university in Ecuador. Critical AI use (M = 4.06/5, SD = 0.60) and verifiable-learning capabilities (M = 3.96/5, SD = 0.60) were high and strongly associated (Spearman’s ρ = 0.641, p < 0.001), whereas GenAI-use frequency was unrelated to either construct. Final-semester students reported higher critical AI use (Holm-adjusted p = 0.004; Cliff’s δ = 0.441), but all were enrolled in Information Technology Regulations; academic stage and discipline were therefore structurally confounded. Revision, applied projects, demonstrations, authentic problems, feedback, and practical workshops received the highest ratings. Qualitative findings emphasised practice, verification, and responsible AI use, while students supported multi-source assessment and explicit rules for permitted AI use. The findings support human-centred assessment designs that prioritise critical governance of AI and credible demonstration of individual learning.

items.title: From aspiration to exhaustion: mental health, motivation, and quality of life among Syrian health professions students in a post-conflict educational landscape
items.abstract: Quality of life (QoL) has emerged as an important indicator of well-being among medical students, particularly in demanding educational environments. Medical education is a highly demanding environment that exposes students to sustained academic and psychological stress, affecting their daily life and mental health. In addition, and due to the conflict, Syrian medical students are exposed to additional economic and psychosocial stressors, all of which necessitated us to evaluate students’ QoL after the end of the Syrian conflict. In this paper, we aimed to evaluate QoL across all its domains and to identify factors associated with variations in students’ well-being. A cross-sectional study was conducted on undergraduate (medical, dental, and pharmacy) students across public and private universities in Syria. Data were collected between November and December 2025 using a self-administered, validated Arabic questionnaire (WHOQOL-BREF). Sociodemographic, academic, lifestyle, and health-related variables were also collected. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlation analyses, and multivariate linear regression models were performed using SPSS. Results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05, with 95% confidence intervals. A total of 1,110 students were included in the analysis. Participants reported the highest QoL scores in the Physical Health domain and the lowest scores in the Environment domain. The overall level of perceived stress was moderate to high. Across all QoL domains, the analysis consistently linked mental disorders and higher perceived stress to lower QoL. Unlike academic difficulties and family pressure, physical activity was robustly associated with better QoL. However, financial difficulties showed the strongest negative association with the Environment domain. Interestingly, gender was a significant associated factorsolely for Social Relationships, favoring female students. This study concluded that key associated factorsof reduced well-being included mental health issues, financial difficulties, and low physical activity, whereas intrinsic motivation and active lifestyles were associated with better outcomes. Our findings emphasize the need to implement immediate policies aimed at enhancing student well-being, especially in conflict-affected countries like Syria. Addressing these issues is crucial for improving students’ QoL and fostering academic and professional resilience. items.title: From Concept to Shape: An Analogue-AI Framework for Architectural Synthesis
items.abstract: Current applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in architectural design education emphasize open-ended ideation and image production, offering limited support for architectural synthesis. This paper proposes a hybrid analogue-AI framework for integrating Generative AI (GenAI) into the architectural design studio, employing GenAI across three stages — problem framing, solution generation, and informed refinement within which the design space repeatedly expands and contracts. Building on Author´s (2025a) AI-assisted workflow and Author’s (2025b) decomposition of the design process into cognitively matched steps, this framework positions GenAI as a support to design reasoning without replacing analogue representation, human agency, or architectural judgement. We argue that constraining GenAI inputs with prior analogue work may support reproducibility, informed creativity and design control, contributing to outcomes that are both original and constructible while addressing recurring AI dependency on open-ended prompting and stylistic iteration.

items.title: From Ethical Framing to Practical Outcomes: Assessing Reliability, Trustworthiness, and Effects on Learning in Early AI Interactions in Higher Education
items.abstract: While AI is rapidly reshaping higher education by offering greater accessibility, personalized learning, and enhanced student engagement, its adoption often surpasses institutional capacity to adapt governance, pedagogy, and knowledge practices. This study, part of an ongoing collaboration between the University of North Carolina Wilmington (USA) and the University of Hertfordshire (UK), explores the practical integration of AI in higher education and proposes an Artificial Intelligence Readiness Framework to support curriculum design, assessment, governance, and knowledge management. The paper presents an exploratory case study of guided AI use in a large postgraduate taught module involving over 300+ international students at the University of Hertfordshire Business School. Drawing on module-level secondary data and instructor reflections, the study examines student engagement with AI, challenges encountered, and implications for teaching and assessment practice. Preliminary findings suggest that structured AI integration within active learning activities supported idea generation, writing development, and student engagement. However, instructor observations also indicated that some students relied on AI-generated content without sufficient critical evaluation, resulting in weaker alignment with assessment expectations. While students generally disclosed their use of AI, concerns remained regarding overreliance and the development of critical thinking skills. The study offers preliminary practitioner insights and introduces an AI Readiness Framework to support the responsible and pedagogically informed integration of AI into higher education curricula.

items.title: From Late-Stage Assurance to Immersive Testing: Designing a Human Factors (HF) Lab to Test Future Rail Infrastructure
items.abstract: In the past, human factors (HF) in infrastructure projects was often applied later through design reviews and standards-based checks after important design decisions had been made. As transport systems become more complex, HF practice is moving toward earlier, more immersive, and more evidence-based testing of designs before infrastructure is built. This presentation describes the development of a HF Lab Implementation Plan for a large transport infrastructure project. The plan was developed through document review, workshops, analysis of users and key activities, and a targeted literature review. HF lab methods and tools were assessed using a rating framework covering both the robustness of evidence for measuring design against success outcomes and whether each method was fit-for-purpose for the project and Human Centred Design (HCD) topic area.

items.title: From process signals to design decisions: towards a data-driven assistance system for hot bulk forging process design
items.abstract: Abstract The project DatProForge (Data-driven Process Modelling of Drop Forging Processes to Increase Productivity Using Adaptive Tool Design Methodology), conducted within the first funding period of SPP 2422 has established the foundations for an end-to-end digital process chain combining experimentally acquired process data, automated finite element (FE) simulations, radar-based condition monitoring, and data-driven and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The resulting methodology provides the basis for developing an intelligent assistant system for process design and optimisation. The intelligent assistant system employs machine learning (ML) and XAI methods to identify defect risks, determine their key influencing factors in a transparent manner, and generate recommendations for process optimisation and adaptive tool design. Using a hot bulk forging process on a servo screw forging press as a representative use case, the paper demonstrates how research results on sensor systems, radar signal processing, stochastic simulation, underfill prediction, vent-channel optimisation, and data-pipeline modelling can be integrated into a unified assistance system. Particular attention is given to the joint analysis of simulation results and experimentally acquired process data to identify relevant process and machine-related effects and to account for associated uncertainties. The resulting simulation-to-reality transfer approach enables the FE models to be successively refined by incorporating these effects, thereby progressively improving their agreement with the real forging process. Combined with interpretable data-driven models, this approach provides a foundation for robust, data-driven decision-making in process optimisation and adaptive tool design.

items.title: From reactionary to proactive management: The risk posed by whole body vibration in a landfill environment
items.abstract: Landfill operations present a unique and high-risk environment for Whole Body Vibration (WBV). Heavy plant operators—particularly those manoeuvring compactors, excavators across waste—are frequently exposed to high levels of vibration. These are particularly prominent in the side-to-side plane due to the inherent instability of uneven waste surfaces and repetitive operational patterns. This presentation explores the lessons learned over time from a multi-year program dedicated to understanding and mitigating WBV risk, aligning with the conference theme of learning from the past to lead in the present. The evolution of our approach reflects a transition from reactive compliance to proactive, data-driven health management. Initially, risk was viewed through a narrow lens of equipment age and occurrences of injury but exposure assessments revealed that technical specifications alone were insufficient predictors of operator exposure. Through consistent assessments, three critical aspects emerged: the mechanical condition of the seating systems, specific operator training, and the systematic management of health outcomes through early intervention. The outcome from these interventions led to slow change in vibration levels and a downward trend in reported musculoskeletal discomfort such as back pain. Key findings highlight that even new machinery can fail to protect operators if seat suspension is not used correctly or operation of the machines exceeds the capability this engineering control can provide. This session outlines the roadmap we followed in applying the hierarchy of controls to an "invisible" hazard. The takeaway is clear: to ensure we protect the future of worker health, we must move beyond assessments as a snapshot in time and embrace an approach that integrates engineering controls with empowered workers through training along with ongoing health surveillance. By treating all hazards as dynamic rather than static, we can significantly elevate the standard of long-term occupational health.

items.title: From Recursive Self-Improvement to Human-AI Reciprocal Improvement
items.abstract: Recursive self-improvement advances most readily in domains where results can be verified reliably, such as mathematics and coding. Beyond these domains, progress slows as reliable signals for evaluating and guiding improvement become harder to obtain, resulting in a jagged frontier of AI capabilities. Yet even where AI self-improves autonomously, its growing capabilities do not necessarily translate into greater human ability to understand, use and build upon its outputs, challenging both continued human participation and effective oversight. We argue that recursive progress should therefore also encompass the growth of human capabilities. We propose Recursive Reciprocal Improvement (RRI) as a process of human–AI co-evolution, in which AI advances help people develop their abilities to propose worthwhile problems, judge results and contribute to higher-level problem solving, while these evolving capabilities inform subsequent generations of AI. Human capabilities thus become both source and target of recursive progress, with AI and human development mutually reinforcing.

items.title: From replicates to casework: a systematic methodological review of data independence and transportability in artificial intelligence models for complex forensic chemical and biological evidence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine-learning models, is increasingly applied to complex forensic chemical, material, and biological evidence. High reported performance does not itself demonstrate generalization to new forensic material. We conducted a systematic methodological review of 446 reports and 1,005 eligible evaluation regimes, examining independence of final evaluation, physical and biological parent grouping, information leakage, external or shifted testing, and transportability. Following source-based methodological assessment and human adjudication, source-supported leakage was classified in 284/446 reports (63.7%); 36/446 (8.1%) showed strong potential concern, 85/446 (19.1%) had uncertain boundaries, and 41/446 (9.2%) had no identified leakage concern. External or shifted evaluation was reported in 278/446 reports (62.3%), although only 94/278 (33.8%) had an evaluation satisfying five strict criteria for transportability of an unchanged pipeline. At regime level, 135/521 external or shifted evaluations (25.9%) satisfied these criteria. Source-supported leakage occurred in 195/308 Biological reports (63.3%) and 87/133 Chemical/Material reports (65.4%): prevalence ratio 1.033 (95% CI 0.889–1.200). The primary comparison did not identify a significant difference across these domains. Casework claims should therefore be evaluated against the independence of the relevant forensic unit, the complete development–test boundary, the shift actually examined, any target-data adaptation, and the applicable performance denominator.

items.title: Functional portfolio and work-demand configuration in digital marketing jobs under remote-work signaling: a network analysis of job advertisements
items.abstract: Introduction Remote-work labels describe an advertised work arrangement, but whether they accompany different advertised requirements remains unclear. Drawing on signaling theory and work design research, we examine two layers of advertised demand: platform-native functional categories and O*NET-anchored work-style language. Methods The primary analysis uses 550 digital-marketing advertisements from one public LinkedIn dataset, including 220 with an explicit remote-work flag and 330 without a recorded flag. An expanded sample of 1,394 advertisements includes the primary sample and assesses sensitivity to the occupational boundary. Overlap-weighted regression adjusts for role family, seniority, employment type, and description length, with standard errors clustered by employer identifier. The seven-element Work-Style Demand Index (WSDI) measures the breadth of matched work-style signals, rather than their intensity or employees' traits. Results The adjusted WSDI remote-flag contrast was –0.018 (95% CI –0.047 to 0.012); the five-element adaptive/growth subindex (AWDI) contrast was -0.008 (95% CI –0.043 to 0.026). Functional breadth differed by +0.058 categories (95% CI –0.091 to 0.206). These estimates provide no clear evidence of an association and do not establish equivalence. The descriptive networks each retained 10 work-style edges, with six shared edges. A rule-based context check found most matches outside identified benefits/equal-opportunity text, but did not establish construct validity. Discussion The study offers a transparent way to examine how work-arrangement information co-occurs with advertised demands. It distinguishes employer-side text signals from applicants' interpretations and employees' experiences.

items.title: Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence Application in Political Processes: A Russian Perspective
items.abstract: This article is devoted to the analysis of theoretical approaches to understand the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in the political sphere as presented in Russian research of 2023–2026. Based on a comparative analysis of these studies, the paper proposes a systematization of approaches regarding AI role: as a technological tool for optimizing political processes, a source of new risks, and an emerging quasi-subject of political communica-tions. It is demonstrated that these approaches are not mutually exclusive but rather reflect different facets of the same phenomenon. The research identifies a key contradiction between the active integration of AI into public administration and maintaining methodological limitations concerned with agency ambiguity, liability blurring, and trust deficit. The author makes the following conclusion: at the current stage, AI remains an auxil-iary tool lacking full-fledged political agency.

items.title: GenAI and Statistics
items.abstract: Presentation given at the Basel Biometric Society Annual Meeting 2026: Quantitative drug development in the age of AI. Abstract: Use of Generative AI is very common in many domains of specialized expertise, including biostatistics. However, applying GenAI to produce high-quality results in a specialized field - particularly within the high-stakes, regulated environment of the pharmaceutical industry - is far from straightforward. In this presentation, I will discuss practical approaches for using GenAI and agentic tools effectively. Different use cases bring distinct gains and risks. At one end, GenAI can be remarkably effective at strengthening the technical foundations of a project - adding checks, linting, formatting, automated tests, and version control - at low risk and cost. At the other end, when we ask AI to solve complex problems within a specialized domain, meaningful human oversight becomes considerably more difficult. Strong human-in-the-loop controls demand a systematic, deliberate approach across the full workflow - from planning to execution - together with the ability to observe and interpret an agent's actions, judge the reliability of its output, and apply the right technical capabilities, including appropriate skills, tools, agents, and agent harnesses. Developing both the technical skills to use GenAI and a clear understanding of use-case scenarios and their associated risks is essential. Doing so allows us to treat AI as a capable tool and thought partner rather than an opaque black box, and to generate results for which we can confidently take accountability.

items.title: Generative AI And National Education Policy 2020: Transforming the Future of Indian Education—A Review
items.abstract: Generative AI is a game-changer, and its transformative potential is evident in education. India has the opportunity to integrate Generative AI and improve its education system with respect to NEP 2020. The current study critically analyses and reviews the integration of Generative AI into the NEP 2020, and specific areas of competency-based education, multilingual education, teacher professional development, equity, and the integration of educational technology. The study has a structured narrative and thematic synthesis of the published research articles between 2020 and 2025, combined with the provisions of the related official documents of policy. The study mainly focuses on the educational promises of conversational AI, and identifies studies on adoption, research accounts and/or interventions. Depending on the task, context, user and teacher mediation, and available resources, different benefits can be gained. One challenge with the current trend to incorporate Generative AI into education is that educational institutions need to determine the extent to which they accept risks and rely on the technology, and also evaluate the educational benefits and potential harm caused by the technology. The review highlights the importance of longitudinal research in various contexts in India (i.e. school level, region, language, school resources).

items.title: Generative AI Copyright Awareness and Views on Human Creative Contribution in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) raises questions about human creative contribution, copyright in outputs and third-party rights. This study examines responses to copyright-related statements in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh, including a separately described subgroup of 241 law students. The questionnaire asks about recognition of copyright questions, the relevance of human contribution, terms of use, third-party rights and the perceived value of guidance. It does not ask respondents to assign ownership to a specified actor or solve a legal problem; consequently, it does not measure actual copyright knowledge or establish legal ownership. Items were analysed separately using descriptive distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and exploratory rank correlations. In the full sample, 191 respondents (49.6%) endorsed recognising that copyright questions can arise, 223 (57.9%) endorsed the relevance of human contribution, and 303 (78.7%) agreed that clear guidance would improve their responsible use. Among law students, the respective percentages were 51.0%, 60.6% and 80.5%. Overall, 147 respondents endorsed both recognising copyright questions and the potential usefulness of guidance, while 156 endorsed guidance without endorsing recognition. This pattern is not evidence that guidance improves knowledge or behaviour. The article distinguishes statements of awareness and normative expectations from demonstrated legal competence, and recommends scenario-based assessment and documentation of respondent recruitment for future research.

items.title: Generative AI feedback use and English writing self-regulation among Chinese non-English majors: a two-wave study of feedback literacy and writing anxiety
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI chatbots now give students instant commentary on their writing, yet little is known about how engaging with that commentary relates to the self-regulatory capacities on which writing development depends. This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. Methods Non-English-major undergraduates at three universities in Henan Province, China, completed two surveys 12 weeks apart in the 2026 spring semester (wave 1 N = 650; 520 retained, 80.0%). Wave 1 assessed generative AI feedback use and feedback literacy; wave 2 assessed writing anxiety and writing self-regulation. Serial mediation analysis used 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples, with item-level validity checks and re-estimations without item parcels added as sensitivity analyses. Results Generative AI feedback use was positively associated with later writing self-regulation [ c = 0.265, 95% CI (0.190, 0.339)]. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. The direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137). Focal paths kept their signs and significance when item parcels were removed and when only feedback-seeking items defined the predictor. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. The pattern is consistent with a theoretically proposed ordering; the pedagogical suggestions are recommendations only, not demonstrated outcomes. The generative AI feedback use scale is a preliminary study-specific measure.

items.title: Generative AI for the Innovative Design of Intangible Cultural Heritage: A Review of Research by Chinese University Scholars
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) advances rapidly, its potential in the innovative design of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) is becoming increasingly evident. This scoping review examines research on GenAI-enabled ICH design by scholars at Chinese universities. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, it draws on the literature retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoS) and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). Through literature analysis and comparison, the review maps the development of relevant technologies, categorises their design applications, and summarises the evaluation approaches used in the selected studies. The reviewed applications fall into three categories: embroidery, dyeing, and weaving; graphic visual arts; and dimensional objects and product forms. It also identifies persistent challenges, including limited access to high-quality ICH data, insufficient understanding of cultural meanings, and unresolved intellectual-property and ethical concerns. The review highlights the growing use of diffusion models, particularly Stable Diffusion combined with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), while emphasising the continued importance of human expertise and community participation. It concludes by outlining directions for more culturally grounded, ethically responsible, and practically applicable GenAI-assisted ICH design in higher education.

Methods This paper presents a structured overview of the current state of AIGC in higher education, examining its impact on teaching methodologies, instructional design, and student learning experiences. Discussion The article also discusses emerging technologies and trends that are likely to shape the future integration of AIGC in academic contexts, alongside ongoing efforts to develop robust frameworks for the accountable and equitable use of them. items.title: Generative AI Use and Student Well-Being in Higher Education: A Literature Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.
